power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Analyses of burden-effect estimates, effect directions and overlap among top-ranked genes showed similar patterns. To further assess how limited progression power affected the detectability of shared genetic effects, we performed simulations matched to the observed event counts and rare-variant carrier spectrum (Extended Data Fig. 7; Supplementary Notes 6 and 7; Supplementary Table 21). When 25% of progression-associated causal genes were also causal for onset, concordance as low as that observed occurred in 22% of simulations, compared with 1.1% when 50% were shared. These findings were conditional on the simulated effect sizes and genetic architectures and did not directly estimate the extent of underlying genetic sharing between onset and progression. Against this background of low aggregate concordance, three progression associations reached exome-wide significance in UKB: GSDME/DFNA5 with benign prostatic hyperplasia→urinary tract infection, MARCHF7/MARCH7 with CKD→hyperkalaemia, and F13A1 with coronary artery disease (CAD)→myocardial infarction (MI). None showed evidence of association with the corresponding T0→T1 transition (P > 0.36 for all), although differences in statistical power preclude interpreting this as definitive evidence of progression specificity. For GSDME and MARCHF7, progression burden-score HRs were >1 with 95% CIs excluding 1, whereas the corresponding T0→T1 CIs included 1. F13A1, which encodes the catalytic subunit of coagulation factor XIII involved in fibrin clot stabilization, emerged as a biologically plausible candidate for CAD→MI progression. However, this association was driven by variance-component SKAT tests and therefore did not establish a directional effect (Extended Data Fig. 8). The small number of progression discoveries was consistent with the limited carrier information in progression risk sets: only 39% of progression masks had a cumulative MAC ≥50, compared with 86% of onset masks.
table.header: Disease onset and progression show limited detectable rare-variant association sharing

table.text: Calibration and power were evaluated using exome genotypes from 100,000 randomly selected White British UKB participants, preserving realistic population structure and relatedness. Null TTE phenotypes were simulated under censoring rates of 90%, 95% and 99%, and GATE-GENE was evaluated with and without saddlepoint approximation (SPA). Power was evaluated at 90% censoring under three rare-variant causal architectures differing in causal-variant proportions and effect sizes and was compared with SAIGE-GENE+ applied to corresponding incident binary phenotypes using the same participants, genotypes and variant masks. Full generative models, causal architectures and simulation parameters are provided in Supplementary Note 2. To benchmark calibration against an existing gene-based rare-variant TTE method, GATE-STAAR was applied to the same simulated null phenotypes. Because its pipeline required method-specific genotype conversion and substantially larger intermediate files, the controlled comparison was restricted to chromosome 19. We evaluated LoF, missense and synonymous variant groups at maximum MAF thresholds of 1%, 0.1% and 0.01% across 200 null phenotype replicates per censoring level. GATE-STAAR was run using its implemented default ultra-rare-variant collapsing threshold (MAC ≤ 20) and default burden, SKAT and STAAR-O settings.

table.text: Calibration of phenome-wide gene-based time-to-event association testing in UK Biobank. a) Tail-based genomic control factor (𝜆 !.! # ) for gene-level tests as a function of event information across the 300 core incident-onset phenotypes in UKB-EUR participants. Each point represents a phenotype-specific 𝜆 !.! # computed from gene-level P-values for the Cauchy-combined test, shown separately for Burden, SKAT and SKAT-O. The x-axis shows the uncensored proportion (100 -censoring rate; log scale). Solid lines and shaded bands denote the binned median and interquartile range of 𝜆 !.! # within uncensored-percentage bins; numbers above the panel indicate the number of phenotypes per bin. The horizontal line marks 𝜆 !.! # = 1. b) Quantile-quantile (QQ) plots for representative onset endpoints spanning a range of censoring proportions. Expected and observed -log₁₀(P) values are shown for the Cauchy-combined SKAT-O test. The dashed line denotes the null expectation. Observed values were capped at -log₁₀(P) = 20 for visualization; points exceeding the cap are indicated by triangles. Phenotype abbreviations: AD, Alzheimer's disease; AF, atrial fibrillation; CAD, coronary artery disease; HTN, essential hypertension; MPD, myeloproliferative disease. Extended Data Fig 2 | Functional convergence among onsetassociated genes. a, Over-representation analysis of selected pathways among the union of 89 genes implicated by the 107 retained gene-phenotype associations. The x-axis shows the enrichment odds ratio on a logarithmic scale. Point area represents the number of overlapping genes and fill represents -log10(global FDR), calculated across the prespecified primary gene-list-pathway analyses. Asterisks indicate empirical global FDR < 0.05 in permutations using control genes matched on gene size, variant availability and testability. b, Enrichment of representative pathways among genes associated with neoplasm, circulatory-system and genitourinary-system phenotypes. Tile intensity represents -log10(global FDR) and point area represents the number of overlapping genes. Asterisks indicate empirical global FDR < 0.05 in matched-gene permutation analyses. Category sizes are shown below each column. c, Leading phenotype-level contributors to pathways identified by the ranked gene-set analysis across the 300 core phenotypes. Pathwaylevel FDR values were obtained after combining phenotype-specific evidence using Cauchy combination and correcting across all tested pathways. The x-axis shows the phenotype-level ranked-analysis P value. Filled circles indicate associations passing within-phenotype, withincollection FDR < 0.05; open circles indicate the remaining displayed contributors. The four strongest phenotype-level contributors are shown for each pathway. Extended Data Fig 3 | Overlap and functional convergence of rareand common-variant associations with disease onset. a, Germline-likely rare-significant gene count against genome-wide significant clumped commonlocus count across 300 incident-onset phenotypes; points are jittered, line is a linear fit with 95% confidence band. b, Null distribution of the Spearman correlation under 10,000 permutations of rare-gene counts within strata jointly defined by event-count quintile and censoring-rate tertile; dashed line, observed value. c, The 14 positional overlaps, showing the distance from each raresignificant gene to the nearest genome-wide significant common lead variant for the same phenotype. Symbols indicate whether the rare association remained exome-wide significant after conditioning on that lead (filled circle), fell below threshold (open triangle), or had an unstable conditional fit (grey square). Inset, matched permutation distribution of positional overlaps; red line, observed overlap count. d, Conditional against unconditional burden effect estimates for the 12 positionally overlapping gene-phenotype pairs with stable conditional fits; dashed line, identity. e, The six non-redundant pathway clusters shared between the rare-and common-variant analyses in circulatory phenotypes. Dot size indicates the number of contributing genes and colour indicates enrichment significance. Asterisks denote clusters retaining at least two genes after removing TTN, MYH7 and MYBPC3; these three genes contributed 30 of 42 rare gene-term memberships. Extended Data Fig 4 | Representative attained-age delayed-entry survival curves stratified by rare-variant carrier status Attained-age event-free survival curves are shown for a, BRCA2-malignant neoplasm of ovary; b, PALB2-breast cancer in females; c, PKD1-chronic renal failure; and d, TSHR-hypothyroidism. Red and black curves denote rare-variant carriers and non-carriers, respectively; shaded bands indicate 95% confidence intervals, and tick marks denote censoring. Curves were estimated using attained age as the time scale with delayed entry at cohort enrolment. Hazard ratios, 95% confidence intervals and two-sided Wald-test P values are from Cox proportional-hazards models including carrier status and available covariates for sex, birth year and the first 20 genetic principal components. Numbers of participants and incident events in each carrier group are shown within each panel. Extended Data Fig 5 | Controls and complementary measures of gene-level association concordance. a, Gene-level Spearman correlations for positive-control pairs of related onset phenotypes with expected shared association signals; the dashed red line indicates the median correlation among disjoint-pair controls. b, Distribution of gene-level effect-size correlation between T1→T2 and T0→T1 across trajectories; red line, median. c, Fraction of genes with concordant effect sign; red dashed line, 0.5 expected under independence; red line, median. Extended Data Fig 6 | Statistical information and sensitivity of rarevariant progression analyses. a, Null-adjusted gene-level association concordance for transition pairs with minimum event counts of 100, 200 and 500, showing the distribution across comparison pairs. n above the axis gives T1→T2 vs T0→T1 pairs at each threshold. b, Median events per tested gene-mask by minorallele-count stratum and transition class. c, Minimum detectable |𝛽| by MAC stratum, estimated from achieved standard errors; shaded band, interquartile range across masks. Note that MAC is an allele COUNT: because progression risk sets are roughly twenty-fold smaller, the same MAC stratum corresponds to a much higher allele frequency in T1→T2 than in T0→T1, so panel b is not a like-for-like power comparison between transition classes and should be read within a class, not across. The reference line in a represents observed unadjusted onsetprogression concordance (𝜌 = 0.0014), whereas that in c represents null-adjusted concordance (0.0001). c, Partial-sharing continuum. Box plots show simulated null-adjusted onset-progression concordance across 95 replicates per cell, for true shared-gene fractions of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1, under complete and 60% ascertainment of incident T1. Boxes give the median and interquartile range, whiskers 1.5× the interquartile range, and the red line the observed value (+0.0001). Building on recent advances in gene-based rare-variant TTE testing, we developed GATE-GENE for scalable association analysis under highly censored biobank settings. GATE-GENE uses a mixed-effects frailty model 19 and applies saddlepoint approximation (SPA) 20, 21 to sparse singlevariant score statistics before gene-based aggregation, improving type I error control when carrier-event counts are limited (Methods; Supplementary Note 1; Fig. 1). We evaluated burden, SKAT 22 and SKAT-https://paperpile.com/c/f3gNQNDo/aKnM 23 tests across nine prespecified rare-coding masks defined by three MAF cutoffs (1%, 0.1% and 0.01%) and three variant annotation categories (LoF only, LoF plus missense and LoF plus missense plus synonymous) and combined evidence across masks using the Cauchy method 24 . We evaluated calibration using UKB exome genotypes from 100,000 White British participants under null phenotypes with 90%, 95% and 99% censoring (Supplementary Note 2; Supplementary Figs. 1 and 2; Supplementary Table 4). GATE-GENE showed no statistically significant evidence of type I error inflation at the exome-wide threshold across the evaluated censoring levels. At the 𝛼 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶, pooled empirical type I error was 1.4 × 10⁻⁶ for both burden and SKAT (95% CI: 5.3 × 10 -7 -3.1 × 10 -6 ), and 2.9 × 10⁻⁶ for SKAT-O (95% CI: 1.5 × 10 -6 -5.0 × 10 -6 ), and 2.1 × 10⁻⁶ (95% CI: 9.9 × 10 -7 -4.1 × 10 -6 ) for the per-gene Cauchy omnibus test. At the less stringent threshold of 𝛼 = 0.001, residual inflation remained, with observed-to-expected exceedance ratios of 1.11-1.55 at. Without SPA, however, SKAT and SKAT-O became increasingly inflated at 95% and 99% censoring, whereas burden remained approximately calibrated. For comparison, we evaluated GATE-STAAR 13 using null phenotypes generated under the same simulation framework, with the comparison restricted to chromosome 19 (Supplementary Fig. 3). Although GATE-STAAR was simulation-evaluated at censoring levels up to 90%, its SKAT and STAAR-O tests showed substantial type I error inflation at 95% and 99% censoring in our simulations. At 99% censoring and 𝛼 = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶, empirical type I error reached 1.7 × 10⁻ 4 for SKAT and 8.1 × 10⁻ 5 for STAAR-O, corresponding to 69.4-fold and 32.3-fold inflation, respectively, whereas the burden test remained near nominal at 3.0 × 10⁻ 6 . A similar pattern was observed at 𝛼 = 0.001. Under simulated alternatives, GATE-GENE also gained modest but consistent power over matched incident case-control analysis using SAIGE-GENE+ 24, 25 . At the exome-wide threshold, SKAT-O power was 24.0%, 58.5% and 66.6% across the three causal architectures, compared with 22.1%, 54.9% and 61.5% for SAIGE-GENE+, respectively (paired P ≤ 1.2 × 10 -6 in all scenarios; Supplementary Fig. 4; Supplementary Tables 5 and 6). Together, these results support the calibration of GATE-GENE at exome-wide significance thresholds under extreme censoring, with modest gains in power when event timing provides additional information.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 2 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

#### Data Files

#### Descriptives Overview

We found 6 columns with at least one missing value.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1038 columns across 6 data files.
#### Issues Identified

1 file/column combination has at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = "example_survival_groupTest_out.txt", Column = "MAC", Issues = "🔒 Personally Identifying Information — Column name suggests personal information (matched: mac)"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 6 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 7 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 7 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.
